name: CASE × Ama La Vida
oneLiner: Pricing and retention strategy for a virtual career-coaching firm, read from its members' plan changes.

context.partner: Ama La Vida, through CASE (Consulting Advising Student Enterprise)

brief.problem: Ama La Vida sells career coaching as memberships and wanted new prices by June without pushing members out. At every renewal a member can continue, stop or downgrade. I was one of three analysts on pricing & retention.
brief.solution: Follow the downgrades, not just the cancellations: a cancellation says someone left, not how much of the plan they still wanted. From 2,000+ plan changes in ALV's history, analysed in R, I traced when members switched, in which direction and to what.
brief.impact: Plan changes ran one way: down — 69–83% of moves out of the monthly plans ended on the cheapest virtual plan. My charts became two slides of the client deck: a $250-a-session ceiling, and members keeping their price by renewing for 12 months.

blocks.title: Raise prices without pushing members out
blocks.text:
Ama La Vida (ALV) sells one-on-one career coaching over video, as memberships. In January 2025 its founders brought CASE, a Northwestern student consulting group, three asks: benchmark what comparable coaching costs, recommend new prices to be in place by June, and plan how to tell current members.

We split into three workstreams — competitors, pricing & retention, and rollout. I was one of three analysts on pricing & retention: the half of the question about keeping members once the prices change.

blocks.title: The cheapest of four similar coaching firms
blocks.text:
ALV coaches for long-range career direction rather than résumé fixes, and priced by plan: two sessions a month for $379 — $189.50 a session — or 12- and 24-session bundles at $1,933 and $3,638. Our competitor workstream found three firms with a similar pitch charging $225 to $450 a session, so there was room to charge more.

The catch: at every renewal, a member can continue, stop, or downgrade to one session a month or a cheaper community plan.

media.caption: From the final client deck: ALV against three firms with a similar pitch (competitor workstream's slide).

blocks.title: Two datasets, one arriving mid-project
blocks.text:
We worked from ALV's own records. First, cancellation files from 2020 to 2024, each with the reason the member gave. Then, in mid-February, an export of membership history: every move from one plan to another, more than 2,000 of them. I did my analysis in R.

The files needed work before they could talk — plan names typed inconsistently, some members missing a start date — and the revenue-by-product data our workstream requested in January never shows as received in the request tracker.

blocks.title: Follow the downgrades, not just the cancellations
blocks.text:
My first task was to test, with a small churn model, whether the reasons members gave for cancelling tracked the plan they were on. Useful for retention, but it couldn't settle price: a cancellation says someone left, not how much of the plan they still wanted.

So when the plan-change history arrived in February, I turned to the members who hadn't quit: when they switched, in which direction, and to what. A downgrade is a member telling you what a plan is worth to them — the price signal cancellations can't give.

blocks.title: Plan changes ran one way: down
blocks.text:
The history was lopsided: downgrades outnumbered upgrades and unchanged renewals many times over. And the moves went down the ladder, mostly to the virtual plan — 69% of changes out of the one-month subscription, 75% out of 2×-monthly and 83% out of 1×-monthly ended there, while 55% of changes out of 4×-monthly stepped down to 2×.

Our project manager read my first charts and asked for exactly those percentages; my charts on where members moved became two slides of the final client deck.

media.caption: Final client deck: every plan change by type.
Where members moved by plan length — my chart, restyled for the deck.
Where members moved by session frequency — my chart, restyled for the deck.

blocks.title: Raise the ceiling, and reward staying up
blocks.text:
The final deck joined two findings. From the benchmark: a $250 ceiling per session with the old bundle discounts kept, taking 12 sessions from $1,933 to $2,550 and 24 from $3,638 to $4,800. From my workstream: since members trade down, make staying up worth it — existing members keep their price by renewing for 12 months; new members get bigger discounts for more sessions and longer terms.

My own notes had argued for changing discounts instead of raising every price. The team did both.

media.caption: The recommended ceiling and bundle prices (final client deck).
The plan picker we proposed for ALV's website: choose a frequency, then a length.

blocks.title: Test the ceiling on members, not rivals
blocks.text:
Two things I'd do differently. The $250 ceiling rests on four firms' list prices, not on how ALV's own members respond; the phased rollout we proposed — loyal members first, then everyone — could double as the price test, if downgrades are tracked cohort by cohort.

And my early churn model deserved more suspicion. Every record in that file was a cancellation, so "churn" had to be defined from tenure — and tenure then "predicted" it. I'd rebuild it on what's known the day someone signs up.
